lesson.title: From Uncuttable to Understood: The History of Atomic Theory
lesson.summary: Atomic theory developed over more than two thousand years through a series of experiments and revised models, each one correcting a specific flaw in the picture of the atom that came before it.
lesson.body:
The idea that matter is made of atoms did not arrive as one sudden discovery. It developed over more than two thousand years, each new model built to fix a problem that evidence exposed in the one before it. The earliest version came from the Greek philosopher Democritus, around 400 BCE, who proposed that matter could not be divided infinitely and must reach some smallest, uncuttable particle he called atomos, the root of the word atom. This idea, though remarkably close to the truth, was pure philosophical reasoning with no experimental support, and was set aside for centuries favoring Aristotle's view that matter was continuous and built from four elements: earth, air, fire, and water.

Atomic theory reentered science on solid experimental footing with John Dalton in the early 1800s. Working from measurements of how elements combine in fixed mass ratios, Dalton proposed that all matter is made of atoms, that atoms of one element are identical to each other but different from atoms of any other element, that atoms combine in simple whole number ratios to form compounds, and that atoms are neither created nor destroyed in chemical reactions. Dalton pictured the atom as a solid, indivisible sphere, essentially a featureless billiard ball, a model that explained the data of the time though later shown incomplete.

The billiard ball model held for nearly a century until J.J. Thomson's 1897 cathode ray experiments discovered the electron, a particle far smaller and lighter than any atom, carrying a negative charge. This directly contradicted Dalton's assumption that atoms were indivisible, since electrons were clearly a piece of something smaller inside the atom. Thomson responded with the plum pudding model: a sphere of diffuse positive charge with electrons scattered through it like plums in a pudding, explaining where the negative electrons came from while keeping the atom neutral overall.

The plum pudding model fell apart because of a specific experiment: Ernest Rutherford's gold foil experiment, published in 1911. Rutherford's team fired positively charged alpha particles at an extremely thin gold foil, expecting only slight deflection if Thomson's model was correct. Instead, while most particles passed straight through, a small fraction deflected at large angles, and a very small number bounced almost straight back. Rutherford concluded that an atom's positive charge and most of its mass must be concentrated in an extremely small, dense nucleus, with the rest of the atom mostly empty space through which most alpha particles passed undisturbed. This nuclear model directly set up the modern picture of protons and neutrons in a central nucleus surrounded by electrons occupying the far larger volume around it.

Niels Bohr refined the nuclear model further in 1913, proposing that electrons occupy fixed energy levels rather than drifting anywhere around the nucleus, jumping between levels by absorbing or releasing precise energy, an idea developed to explain the colors of light emitted by energized hydrogen gas. Bohr's neat circular orbits were later replaced by the more accurate quantum mechanical model, which describes electrons as probability regions called orbitals rather than fixed paths, but his core insight, that electron energy is quantized rather than continuous, remains central to how chemists understand atomic structure and bonding today. This sequence, each theory built by testing and correcting the one before it, is a clear example of the scientific method working across generations, not in one afternoon in a lab.
